chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa, and Abu Ali al-Ash'ari, from Muhammad ibn al-Jabbar, all from Ibn Fazzal, from Ali ibn Uqba, from Hammad ibn Bashir, who said:

I heard Abu Abdullah (peace be upon him) saying: The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) said: Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: 'Whoever humiliates a friend of Mine, he has prepared himself for war against Me; and no servant draws near to Me with anything more beloved to Me than what I have made obligatory upon him, and indeed, he continues to draw near to Me with voluntary acts until I love him.'

So when I love him, I become his hearing with which he hears, and his sight with which he sees, and his tongue with which he speaks, and his hand with which he grasps. If he supplicates to Me, I answer him, and if he asks Me, I give him.
And I do not hesitate about anything I intend to do as I hesitate about the death of the believer; he dislikes death, and I dislike disappointing him.
ai.seo_question: What is the spiritual status of a believer who combines obligatory and voluntary acts of worship according to Hadith al-Qudsi?
ai.summary: This foundational hadith qudsi, recorded in Al-Kafi, establishes the spiritual hierarchy of divine love, linking the fulfillment of obligatory duties (fara'id) with voluntary acts (nawafil) to achieve the state of 'God's faculties' (sami'uhu wa basaruhi). In Shia scholarship, this is often interpreted through the lens of the Imams as the perfect exemplars of this state, where divine guidance manifests through human agency. The hadith concludes with a unique theological insight: God’s only hesitation in answering a believer's prayer is granting their wish for death, as He dislikes the sorrow of their passing.
